title: Flag raisings after the Spanish-American War
summary: Barber Johnny Hummel hires him and others to play at a flag raising. The craze spreads and they play free for friends.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Well, they just played parties, you understand? Parties, yeah. Mm-hmm. Now in 1998 they had a lot of flag raisins. I don't know if that, if they took that on in the north, or in the east, or even in the west, like they did here in the city of New Orleans. But right after the Spanish-American War, man, there was flag raisins. I believe I told you about that, didn't I?
Yeah, you tell Mr. Russell, or another, have it on here. I'd like to hear about it too.
I thought about the flag raisin, because you put it on that tape back. Yeah. Tell Mr. Russell about the flag raisin when you told us.

Oh, yeah. Well, the first flag raisin I believe they had was a barber, Johnny Hommel. He used to like music. And he says, I'm gonna, I'm gonna have a flag raisin here, such a night. And he said, I wanna see if you fellas, he said, you and Huston, and, and, uh, John F. Womerson, and Albert Six, you'll come over here and play. He said, if there's any charges, I'll pay you whatever's necessary. So, all right. We told him it was all right. It was a patriotic layout, and, we'd play. For nothing. I said, that is, I was playing my part for nothing. So, I told them fellas, and they agreed too, so it didn't cost them anything. You know, the first thing you know, next week, there's somebody in the next block, raising the flag. And Christ, there was flag raisin regularly, it was common then. Just like when the women cut their hair off. You understand?
There was, one woman see the other with her hair cut off, she's gonna get her damn hair cut off, and that's the way it was with that flag raisin then.

Well, did they do that so that you wouldn't, they wouldn't have to pay the musicians, or what? Did they ever pay them? Well, you know, not all of them. Not all of them. We didn't play for everybody. I thought maybe they'd try to make it a patriotic affair, so they wouldn't have to pay the fellas, you know.
somehow when you knew them, you'd play for nothing, you know.

We'd charge them dough. Yeah. You know, people that we didn't know so well. Sure. But, Johnny Hummel, he used to be a, he had children too, and he was an older man than I was. But he had a barbershop down there, and he had a big trade. And when he told us about the flag raising, I told him, I said, well I'll see them fellas that all the groups come for me to play with them. I said, I'll see them. And I said, if it's agreeable, I'll get them to come here. So they agreed, and went there and played.
Did they put up a big flag pole? Yeah, they put up a flag pole,
a foundation, you know, a concrete foundation. Right down on the ground, in the building. Yes, and then they'd put the pole in, and had the, what you call it, high stuff, the flag.
